newsitem.title: USA: Hurricane fears abate, forcing US cash crudes down.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane fears abate, forcing US cash crudes down.

text.p: Hurricane Danny left U.S. Gulf oil installations unscathed as the storm travelled by Louisiana Friday, resulting in sharp losses for crude markets held aloft by precautionary buying on fears of Danny's wrath.

Cash crude outrights faltered badly as the week-ending session progressed, submitting to a continuous flow of hurricane reports, and news the Colombian Cano-Limon pipeline and field production were back in swing after being shut by a rebel bombing campaign on July 6.

Traders also noted that the impending completion of the laborious process to restart Iraqi oil sales weighed on values. U.N. sanctions committee members said on Thursday that the timetable for approving an aid distribution plan under the "oil-for-food" accord would likely put Iraqi oil back on world markets by the first week of August.
"You really had the elimination of the bullish weather story and Colombia, and the thoughts Iraqi oil was now only a few weeks away," said a Gulf trader.

August West Texas Intermediate/Cushing talked late in the session some 70 cents lower at $19.15-25 a barrel. September WTI/Cushing regained a strong premium to the front, with the August/September spread, or roll, measured at -24 cents.

Even though much oil and gas production in the Gulf regions around Louisiana were shut-in ahead of Danny's passing, the markets declined on sentiment the situation was not a major disruption to supply.
Friday afternoon the National Weather Service in Miami said the storm was expected to range along the Mississippi/Alabama coast in the next 24 hours.
Little change in the storm's strength is forecast until it moves well inland, probably some time Saturday, when it will weaken. Sustained winds were clocked at 75 mph (120 kmph).
Grades saw WTI/Midland talk late at 27-23 cents under the August benchmark, and Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James at 20-23 cents over the same marker.
Sweet grades were gradually returning to less lofty levels as the threat of disruption to offshore facilities and Capline throughput was mainly eliminated.

Sour crudes were modestly traded, selling in a range of $1.20-18 under August WTI, around 10-15 cents weaker than the firmest deals seen earlier in the week. Colombian supply disruptions had bolstered WTS and Eugene Island, but now that force majeure was ending on Cano output, the market faded.
